---
title: "Python Packages"
---

In the [Whole Game](whole_game.qmd) chapter, a single `uv init --package` command created a `pyproject.toml` file, a `src/pyap/` folder, and a build system, and we moved on without looking closely at any of them. This chapter slows that step down. We'll start with the loose files from the end of the [Shiny for Python](shiny.qmd) chapter and turn them into an installable package one branch at a time, so each new file has a reason to exist before we add it.

If you've read [Shiny App-Packages](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/), you've seen this conversion before. In R, we added the mandatory fields to `DESCRIPTION`, configured the `.Rproj` build tools, and ran `usethis::create_package()`. The Python version follows the same arc, and I'll point out where the two languages line up (and where they don't) along the way.

The diagram below shows the three branches we'll build in this chapter, starting from the `02.3_proj-app` branch:


The first two branches change how the project describes and installs its dependencies, but the app code doesn't move. Only the last branch turns `pyap` into a package.

## What is a Python package?

In R, the word "package" covers everything at once. `sap` is the folder we develop, the thing we install with `install.packages()`, and the name we pass to `library()`. Python splits these into three separate ideas, and the documentation uses the word "package" for two of them. I've found this is the single biggest source of confusion for R developers reading Python packaging docs, so it's worth getting the terms straight before we write any files.

### Modules, packages, and distributions

The [Python Packaging User Guide glossary](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/glossary/) defines the three terms below:

* **Module**: a single `.py` file. `utils.py` is a module, and `from utils import scatter_plot` imports a function from it.
* **Import package**: a folder of modules with an `__init__.py` file. In the `03.3_create-package` branch, `src/pyap/` becomes an import package, and the import changes to `from pyap.utils import scatter_plot`.
* **Distribution package**: the installable archive built from a project (and described by its `pyproject.toml`). When we run `pip install shiny`, we're installing a distribution.

The names of an import package and a distribution package usually match, but they don't have to. For example, we install [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/) with `pip install scikit-learn`, but we import it with `import sklearn`. Shiny keeps them the same (`pip install shiny` and `import shiny`), and so will `pyap`.

Distributions come in two formats. A source distribution (or sdist) is a `.tar.gz` archive of the project's source files, and a wheel is a pre-built `.whl` archive that can be installed without a build step.[^pkgs-dist-formats] We saw both in the `dist/` folder at the end of the [Whole Game](whole_game.qmd) chapter.

[^pkgs-dist-formats]: An sdist is roughly the Python version of a bundled R package (the `.tar.gz` file from `devtools::build()`), and a wheel is roughly a binary package.

By these definitions, the `02.3_proj-app` branch holds two *modules* (`app.py` and `utils.py`) and *no packages* of either kind. By the end of this chapter, it will hold one import package (`pyap`) that `uv` can build into a distribution (also `pyap`).

The 'rough' mappings above deserve at least a sentence of explanation (to the best of my knowledge):

* **`NAMESPACE` and `__init__.py`**: Python doesn't have a file that lists exports. Every name in a module is importable unless it starts with an underscore, and `__init__.py` controls what's available directly from `pyap` (along with the optional `__all__` list). Imports from other packages are declared in `pyproject.toml`, not `__init__.py`.

* **`man/` and docstrings**: docstrings live *on the objects themselves*, so there's no generated help folder. The [Documentation](document.qmd) chapter covers them.

* **`inst/` and package data**: non-Python files (like `movies.csv`) can live inside `src/pyap/` and be installed with the code. The [Data](data.qmd) chapter covers how to read them.

* **`.Rbuildignore` and build settings**: the build backend decides which files go into a distribution, and most backends accept include and exclude settings in a `[tool.*]` table.

This chapter covers the top row of the diagram (`pyproject.toml`, `__init__.py`, and `src/pyap/`) and the lockfile. The remaining rows have their own chapters.

## What is `pyproject.toml`?

`pyproject.toml` is the file that tells Python tools what a project is, what it depends on, and how to build it.[^pkgs-description] Every modern Python packaging tool reads it, including `pip`, `uv`, and the build backends we'll cover below.

[^pkgs-description]: `pyproject.toml` is the closest Python equivalent of the `DESCRIPTION` file. It also absorbs some of the jobs we'd hand to `.Rproj` build settings and package configuration in R.

::: {.callout-note title="Why pyproject.toml replaced setup.py" collapse="true"}

For most of Python's history, package metadata lived in a `setup.py` file. `setup.py` is a Python script that calls `setuptools.setup()` with the package name, version, and dependencies. Because it's executable code, tools had to run it to learn anything about the package, and they couldn't run it without first installing `setuptools`. A static `setup.cfg` file was added later, but it only worked with `setuptools`.

`requirements.txt` was never a package metadata file at all. It's a list of packages for `pip` to install into an environment, which is why we used it in the [Shiny for Python](shiny.qmd) chapter. It can't tell anyone the name or version of our project, and nothing in it describes how to build a distribution.

Three Python Enhancement Proposals (PEPs) replaced these files with a single declarative one:

* [PEP 518](https://peps.python.org/pep-0518/): introduced `pyproject.toml` and the `[build-system]` table, so tools know what to install before building a package.
* [PEP 517](https://peps.python.org/pep-0517/): defined a standard interface between installers and build backends, so `setuptools` became one option among many.
* [PEP 621](https://peps.python.org/pep-0621/): standardized the `[project]` table for metadata, so any backend reads the name, version, and dependencies from the same place.

You'll still find `setup.py` in older projects, and `requirements.txt` is still common for deployment (we'll come back to this below). New packages only need `pyproject.toml`. The [Writing your pyproject.toml](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/writing-pyproject-toml/) guide in the Python Packaging User Guide is the canonical reference for the file.

:::

### Reading TOML

You don't have to learn a new configuration language to read `pyproject.toml`, but it helps to know three rules of [TOML](https://toml.io/en/) (Tom's Obvious Minimal Language):

1. A name in square brackets (like `[project]`) starts a table, and everything below it belongs to that table until the next one starts.
2. Inside a table, each line is a `key = value` pair. Strings are quoted, and lists go in square brackets.
3. A dot in a table name nests it, so `[project.scripts]` is a table inside `[project]`.

TOML is just a stricter version of the `Field: value` format in a `DESCRIPTION` file. The sections below cover the tables we'll see in this book.

### `[project]`

The `[project]` table holds the package metadata. The `pyproject.toml` from the [Whole Game](whole_game.qmd) chapter is a good example:

```toml
[project]
name = "pyap"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A Shiny for Python app-package"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Jane Doe", email = "jane.doe@email.io" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "matplotlib>=3.11.2",
    "numpy>=2.5.3",
    "shiny>=1.8.0",
]
```

Only `name` is strictly required, and `version` is required unless a tool computes it for us. That's a much shorter list than the seven mandatory fields in an R `DESCRIPTION` file.[^pkgs-desc-fields] `requires-python` sets the Python versions the package supports, and `dependencies` lists the distributions it needs at runtime, using the same version specifiers as `requirements.txt`.

[^pkgs-desc-fields]: `dependencies` plays the role of `Imports` in `DESCRIPTION`, and `requires-python` plays the role of `Depends: R (>= 4.1.0)`.

### `[build-system]`

The `[build-system]` table tells installers which build backend to use and how to install it:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.12.23,<0.13.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
```

`requires` lists the packages needed to build the project, and `build-backend` names the object that does the building. We'll cover backends in their own section below. For now, the important point is what this table signals: a `pyproject.toml` with a `[build-system]` table describes something that can be built and installed as a package.

### `[dependency-groups]`

The `[dependency-groups]` table ([PEP 735](https://peps.python.org/pep-0735/)) holds dependencies we need while developing the package, but that users don't need to run it:

```toml
[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=9.1.1",
]
```

Dependency groups aren't included in the package metadata, so installing `pyap` never installs `pytest`.[^pkgs-suggests] `uv` installs the `dev` group by default when it syncs the project. The [Dependencies](dependencies.qmd) chapter covers groups in more detail.

[^pkgs-suggests]: `[dependency-groups]` is roughly the `Suggests` field, which is where R packages list `testthat`. The difference is that `Suggests` is published with the package and dependency groups are not.

### `[project.scripts]`

The `[project.scripts]` table registers terminal commands that are created when the package is installed. Each key is a command name, and each value points to a function as `module:function`:

```toml
[project.scripts]
pyap = "pyap.app:run"
```

This is the entry we added in the [Whole Game](whole_game.qmd) chapter so that typing `pyap` in a terminal launches the app. R packages don't have a direct equivalent. We won't add a launch function in this chapter, and the [Launch](launch.qmd) chapter covers entry points in detail.

### `[tool.*]`

Any table that starts with `tool.` belongs to a specific tool, and every other tool ignores it. This lets a project keep its configuration in one file instead of a folder of dotfiles. For example, `pytest` reads its settings from `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`:

```toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
```

We'll add `[tool.*]` tables as we adopt new tools throughout the book. For a real world example of all these tables working together, the [`pyproject.toml` for `py-shiny`](https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/blob/main/pyproject.toml) is worth skimming. It's much longer than ours, but it's built from the same pieces.

::: {.callout-note title="pyproject.toml and Posit Connect" collapse="true"}

`rsconnect-python` can deploy directly from a `pyproject.toml`. [`rsconnect deploy pyproject`](https://docs.posit.co/rsconnect-python/deploying/) reads a `[tool.rsconnect]` table for the app settings:

```toml
[tool.rsconnect]
app_mode = "python-shiny"
entrypoint = "app.py"
```

The `[project]` dependencies provide the dependency list, and a pinned `uv.lock` or `requirements.txt` can be supplied with `--requirements-file`. [Connect Cloud](https://docs.posit.co/connect-cloud/how-to/python/shiny-python.html) still expects a `requirements.txt` with `app.py` as the primary file, so a `requirements.txt` can come back at deployment time (uv can generate one from `uv.lock` with `uv export`). The [Deploy](deploy.qmd) section covers both.

:::

## Writing `pyproject.toml`

The first branch replaces `requirements.txt` with a hand written `pyproject.toml`. Check out the `03.1_pyproject` branch to follow along:

```bash
git checkout 03.1_pyproject
```

The app code doesn't change. The branch deletes `requirements.txt`, adds `pyproject.toml`, and updates the install instructions in `README.md`:

```default
pyap/
├── .gitignore
├── .vscode/
│   └── settings.json
├── README.md
├── app.py
├── movies.csv
├── pyproject.toml
└── utils.py
```

### Adding project metadata

The full `pyproject.toml` in this branch is below:

```toml
[project]
name = "pyap"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A Shiny for Python app-package"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Martin Frigaard" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "matplotlib>=3.8.0",
    "numpy>=1.26.0",
    "pandas>=2.1.0",
    "shiny>=1.2.0",
]
```

The `dependencies` list holds the same four entries (and lower bounds) as the old `requirements.txt`, sorted alphabetically. The rest of the table gives the project a name, a version, and a supported Python version, which `requirements.txt` had no way to record.

The file doesn't have a `[build-system]` table yet. This is deliberate. `pyap` is still a folder of loose modules with nothing to build, so we're only using `pyproject.toml` to describe the project and its dependencies.

### Installing from pyproject.toml

uv can install the `dependencies` from a `pyproject.toml` with the same `-r` flag we used for `requirements.txt`:

```bash
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r pyproject.toml
```

If you already have a `.venv/` from the earlier branches, you can skip `uv venv`. The install command only reads the `dependencies` list. It doesn't try to install `pyap` itself (which is good, because there's nothing to install yet).

We can confirm the environment still works by launching the app the same way as before:

```bash
shiny run --reload --launch-browser app.py
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Positron"}

Positron watches for `pyproject.toml` and `requirements.txt` files. If it finds one in a project that doesn't have a virtual environment yet, it [offers to create one with uv](https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-07-08_positron-uv/) and install the dependencies for us. If uv can't find a Python installation, the Start Session button also includes an option to install Python with uv.

:::

## Managing the project with `uv`

In the `03.1_pyproject` branch, `uv` is only acting as a faster `pip`: we create the environment, activate it, and tell it what to install. The `03.2_uv` branch hands the whole job to uv's project commands. `uv` is also the first option listed on the [Shiny for Python install page](https://shiny.posit.co/py/get-started/install.html). Check out the `03.2_uv` branch to follow along:

```bash
git checkout 03.2_uv
```

The app code and `pyproject.toml` are unchanged. The branch adds `.python-version` and `uv.lock`, removes both from `.gitignore` so they're committed, and updates the commands in `README.md`:

```default
pyap/
├── .gitignore
├── .python-version
├── .vscode/
│   └── settings.json
├── README.md
├── app.py
├── movies.csv
├── pyproject.toml
├── utils.py
└── uv.lock
```

### Pinning Python

`requires-python` in `pyproject.toml` sets the range of Python versions the project supports, but it doesn't choose one. `uv python pin` records the exact version `uv` should use for this project in a `.python-version` file:

```bash
uv python pin 3.12
```

Returns: 

```default
Pinned `.python-version` to `3.12`
```

The file holds a single line:

```default
3.12
```

If Python 3.12 isn't installed, `uv` downloads it the first time it needs it (we covered `uv python install` in the [Introduction](intro.qmd)).

### Syncing the environment

`uv sync` reads `pyproject.toml`, resolves the dependencies, and makes `.venv/` match the result:

```bash
uv sync
```

```default
Resolved 45 packages in 127ms
Checked 43 packages in 0.48ms
```

This one command does the work of the three we ran in the previous branch. `uv` creates `.venv/` if it doesn't exist (or reuses it if it does), writes `uv.lock`, and installs the locked versions into the environment. We don't need to activate the environment first, and we don't need to tell `uv` which file to read.

::: {.callout-warning title="uv sync removes packages"}

`uv sync` makes the environment match the lockfile exactly, which means it uninstalls anything that isn't listed. If you installed extra packages into `.venv/` in earlier branches (like `polars` from the callout in the [Shiny for Python](shiny.qmd) chapter), `uv sync` removes them. From this branch on, add packages with `uv add`, which updates `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, and `.venv/` in one step. The [Dependencies](dependencies.qmd) chapter covers `uv add` in detail.

:::

To run a command inside the environment, we prefix it with `uv run`:

```bash
uv run shiny run --reload --launch-browser app.py
```

`uv run` checks that `.venv/` is in sync with `uv.lock` before running the command, so most of the time we don't need to call `uv sync` ourselves.

### `uv.lock`

`uv.lock` records the exact version of every package in the environment, including the dependencies of our dependencies. `pyproject.toml` says `pandas>=2.1.0`, and `uv.lock` says which `pandas` was installed. uv writes the lockfile for every platform at once, so a lockfile created on macOS installs the same versions on Windows or Linux.

We don't edit `uv.lock` by hand, but it's worth knowing what's in it. The diagram below compares how a dependency moves from declaration to installation in R (with `renv`) and in Python (with uv):

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: 'From declared dependency to installed package'
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"14px"}}}%%

flowchart TB
    subgraph RDeps["R"]
    direction TB
        RDesc["<code>DESCRIPTION</code><br/><code>Imports</code>"]
        RLib[("project library<br/><code>renv/library/</code>")]
        RLock["<code>renv.lock</code>"]
        RDesc -->|"<code>install_deps()</code>"| RLib
        RLib -->|"<code>renv::snapshot()</code>"| RLock
    end

    subgraph PyDeps["Python"]
    direction TB
        PyProj["<code>pyproject.toml</code><br/><code>dependencies</code>"]
        PyLock["<code>uv.lock</code>"]
        PyVenv[("project environment<br/><code>.venv/</code>")]
        PyProj -->|"<code>uv lock</code>"| PyLock
        PyLock -->|"<code>uv sync</code>"| PyVenv
    end

    classDef rStyle fill:#2c5282,stroke:#63b3ed,color:#fff
    classDef pyStyle fill:#744210,stroke:#f6ad55,color:#fff

    class RDesc,RLib,RLock rStyle
    class PyProj,PyLock,PyVenv pyStyle
```

The order of the last two steps is the important difference. `renv::snapshot()` records whatever is already installed in the project library, so the lockfile follows the environment. `uv` resolves `uv.lock` from `pyproject.toml` first and then installs from it, so the environment follows the lockfile.[^pkgs-renv-restore] `uv sync` runs the `uv lock` step for us whenever `pyproject.toml` changes.

[^pkgs-renv-restore]: `uv sync` on a fresh clone is the equivalent of `renv::restore()`.

::: {.callout-note title="Commit uv.lock and .python-version"}

The `.gitignore` in earlier branches listed `.python-version` and `uv.lock`. The `03.2_uv` branch removes both entries, so anyone who clones the repository and runs `uv sync` gets the same Python version and the same package versions we used.

:::

### Non-package projects

The `pyproject.toml` in this branch still doesn't have a `[build-system]` table, and `uv` notices. `uv` treats a project without a build system as a non-package project: it installs the dependencies into `.venv/`, but it doesn't install the project itself.[^pkgs-tool-uv-package] The lockfile entry for `pyap` reflects this with a `virtual` source (trimmed below):

[^pkgs-tool-uv-package]: `uv` lets us override this choice with `package = true` or `package = false` in a `[tool.uv]` table, but the `[build-system]` table is the standard signal.

```toml
[[package]]
name = "pyap"
version = "0.1.0"
source = { virtual = "." }
dependencies = [
    { name = "matplotlib" },
    { name = "numpy" },
    { name = "pandas" },
    { name = "shiny" },
]
```

We can confirm `pyap` isn't installed by trying to import it:

```bash
uv run python -c "import pyap"
```

```default
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyap'
```

This error is expected. A non-package project is a perfectly good way to manage an app that only ever runs from its own folder, and many Shiny for Python apps never need more. We want `pyap` to be importable (and testable, and installable), though, so the next step is giving it something to build.

## Build backends

A build backend is the tool that turns a project's source files into a distribution. When an installer like `pip` or `uv` needs to build a package, it reads `[build-system]`, installs the packages listed in `requires` into a temporary environment, and asks the `build-backend` to produce a wheel or an sdist.[^pkgs-r-cmd-build] Installers and backends only talk through the interface defined in PEP 517, so any installer works with any backend.

[^pkgs-r-cmd-build]: R has one build tool built into the language (`R CMD build` and `R CMD INSTALL`, which `devtools` calls for us). Python lets each project choose its own.

The `[build-system]` table for four common backends is below:

| Backend | `requires` | `build-backend` |
|---|---|---|
| [uv_build](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/build-backend/) | `["uv_build>=0.12.23,<0.13.0"]` | `"uv_build"` |
| [Hatchling](https://hatch.pypa.io/) | `["hatchling"]` | `"hatchling.build"` |
| [setuptools](https://setuptools.pypa.io/) | `["setuptools>=61"]` | `"setuptools.build_meta"` |
| [Flit](https://flit.pypa.io/) | `["flit_core"]` | `"flit_core.buildapi"` |

For a pure Python package like `pyap`, these backends produce nearly the same wheel. They differ in their defaults (where they look for the package, which files they include) and in how much they can be configured. `setuptools` is the oldest and the one you'll find in most older projects. Hatchling is the first option in the [Python Packaging User Guide tutorial](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/tutorials/packaging-projects/), and Flit is intentionally minimal.

This book uses `uv_build`, the default backend for `uv init --package` (it's the backend in the [Whole Game](whole_game.qmd) `pyproject.toml`). It's built by the same team as `uv`, it expects the `src/` layout we'll use below, and it needs no configuration for a package like `pyap`. The version range in `requires` should match the version of uv you have installed (check it with `uv --version`), so yours may differ from the one in this chapter.

## Creating the package

The `03.3_create-package` branch turns `pyap` into a package. Check it out to follow along:

```bash
git checkout 03.3_create-package
```

The branch makes three changes: it adds a `[build-system]` table to `pyproject.toml`, it moves the Python code into `src/pyap/`, and it updates the import in `app.py`. The new project structure is below:

```default
pyap/
├── .gitignore
├── .python-version
├── .vscode/
│   └── settings.json
├── README.md
├── movies.csv
├── pyproject.toml
├── src/
│   └── pyap/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── app.py
│       └── utils.py
└── uv.lock
```

R packages need two things to be packages: a `DESCRIPTION` file with the mandatory fields and an `R/` folder. A Python package needs three: a `pyproject.toml` with `name` and `version`, a `[build-system]` table, and an import package for the backend to build. We already have the first, so the sections below add the other two.

### Adding a build system

We'll add the `[build-system]` table to the bottom of `pyproject.toml`. The complete file is below:

```toml
[project]
name = "pyap"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A Shiny for Python app-package"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Martin Frigaard" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "matplotlib>=3.8.0",
    "numpy>=1.26.0",
    "pandas>=2.1.0",
    "shiny>=1.2.0",
]

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.12.23,<0.13.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
```

With this table in place, `uv` stops treating `pyap` as a non-package project. It also tells `uv_build` what to build: by default, `uv_build` looks for an import package with the same name as the project in `src/` (so `src/pyap/__init__.py`).

### Moving the code into `src/pyap/`

Next, we'll create the package folder and move both modules into it:

```bash
mkdir -p src/pyap
mv app.py utils.py src/pyap/
```

`src/pyap/` needs an `__init__.py` file to be an import package. Python runs `__init__.py` the first time `pyap` is imported, so anything defined or imported in it is available as `pyap.<name>`. We don't need to expose anything yet, so the file only holds a docstring describing the package:

```python
"""A Shiny for Python app-package."""
```

Putting the package under `src/` (instead of a `pyap/` folder at the project root) means Python can only import `pyap` after it's installed, not just because it happens to be in the working directory. The [src/ Layout](src_layout.qmd) chapter explains why this protects our tests, and the [Flat Layout](flat_layout.qmd) chapter covers the alternative.

### Updating imports

`app.py` imported `scatter_plot()` with `from utils import scatter_plot`, which worked because `utils.py` was in the same folder as `app.py`. Inside a package, modules import each other using the full package path:

```python
# Run with: uv run shiny run src/pyap/app.py
from shiny import App, ui, render, reactive
import pandas as pd

from pyap.utils import scatter_plot
```

The rest of `app.py` (including `import pandas as pd`) is unchanged, and so is `utils.py`. `pandas`, `matplotlib`, and `shiny` are installed distributions, so they're imported by name exactly as before. Only imports of our own code change.

::: {.callout-warning title="Why not keep from utils import?"}

`shiny run src/pyap/app.py` adds the folder that holds `app.py` to Python's search path, so `from utils import scatter_plot` would still work when we launch the app this way. It breaks as soon as anything imports the app as `pyap.app` (like a test, or the `run_app("pyap.app:app")` launch function from the [Whole Game](whole_game.qmd) chapter), because `utils` isn't a top level module. `from pyap.utils import scatter_plot` works in both cases.

:::

### Where the data file goes

`movies.csv` stays at the project root in this branch. `app.py` still reads it with `pd.read_csv("movies.csv")`, and that relative path is resolved from the folder we launch the app from (not the folder that holds `app.py`). As long as we run the app from the project root, the file is found.

This works, but it's fragile. The wheel is built from `src/pyap/`, so `movies.csv` isn't part of the installed package, and launching the app from any other folder fails. Moving the file into `src/pyap/` doesn't fix the relative path on its own. The [Data](data.qmd) chapter moves `movies.csv` into the package and reads it with `importlib.resources`, which finds the file wherever the package is installed.

### Installing in editable mode

With a build system and an import package in place, `uv sync` now installs `pyap` itself along with its dependencies:

```bash
uv sync
```

```default
Resolved 45 packages in 411ms
      Built pyap @ file:///home/path/to/projects/apps/python/pyap                                 
Prepared 1 package in 10ms
Installed 1 package in 0.96ms
 + pyap==0.1.0 (from file:///home/path/to/projects/apps/python/pyap)
```

`uv` installs the project in editable mode by default. An editable install points Python at the files in `src/pyap/` instead of copying them into `.venv/`, so changes to the code are picked up the next time `pyap` is imported (without reinstalling).[^pkgs-load-all] We only need to sync again when `pyproject.toml` changes. The `pyap` entry in `uv.lock` changes from a `virtual` source to an `editable` one:

[^pkgs-load-all]: An editable install gives us the same quick feedback loop as `devtools::load_all()`.

```toml
[[package]]
name = "pyap"
version = "0.1.0"
source = { editable = "." }
```

The import that failed in the previous branch now works, and `__file__` shows Python is reading `pyap` from our source folder:

```bash
uv run python -c "import pyap; print(pyap.__file__)"
```

```default
/path/to/pyap/src/pyap/__init__.py
```

::: {.callout-note title="Editable installs in the Posit docs"}

The [Shiny for Python custom components guide](https://shiny.posit.co/py/docs/custom-components-pkg.html) packages its project with a `pyproject.toml` and installs it with `uv pip install -e .` during development. The `-e` flag is the `pip` style way to request an editable install, and it's what `uv sync` does for us automatically in a uv project. The guide points to the [Python Packaging User Guide](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/tutorials/packaging-projects/) for building and publishing, which we'll cover in the [PyPI](pypi.qmd) chapter.

:::

### Running the app

The app now lives at `src/pyap/app.py`, so we pass that path to `shiny run`. We'll run it from the project root, so `movies.csv` is found:

```bash
uv run shiny run --reload --launch-browser src/pyap/app.py
```

The app looks and behaves exactly as it did in the `02.3_proj-app` branch. We can confirm the package import is working by changing the x axis dropdown and watching the scatter plot update (the plot comes from `pyap.utils`, so it wouldn't render if the import failed).

## The development loop

Now that `pyap` is a package, the day to day loop of editing, documenting, testing, and building looks different from the R workflow. The diagram below maps the `devtools` functions from the R book to the `uv` and `pytest` commands we'll use in this one:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: 'devtools functions and their uv and pytest counterparts'
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"14px"}}}%%

flowchart LR
    subgraph RLoop["R (devtools)"]
        LA("<code>load_all()</code>")
        DOC("<code>document()</code>")
        TST("<code>test()</code>")
        CHK("<code>check()</code>")
        INS("<code>install()</code>")
        BLD("<code>build()</code>")
    end

    subgraph PyLoop["Python (uv + pytest)"]
        SYNC("<code>uv sync</code><br/>(editable install)")
        DS("docstrings<br/>(no build step)")
        PT("<code>uv run pytest</code>")
        NONE("no single<br/>command")
        UB("<code>uv build</code>")
    end

    LA --> SYNC
    INS --> SYNC
    DOC --> DS
    TST --> PT
    CHK -.->|"roughly"| NONE
    BLD --> UB

    classDef rStyle fill:#2c5282,stroke:#63b3ed,color:#fff
    classDef pyStyle fill:#744210,stroke:#f6ad55,color:#fff

    class LA,DOC,TST,CHK,INS,BLD rStyle
    class SYNC,DS,PT,NONE,UB pyStyle
```

Two R functions collapse into one Python command. `load_all()` and `install()` both become the editable install from `uv sync`, because the installed package and our source files are the same files. `document()` disappears, since docstrings don't need to be rendered into help files before `help()` can read them. `check()` doesn't have a single equivalent; its jobs are split across `pytest`, linters, and type checkers.

The [Development Workflow](development.qmd) chapter covers this loop in practice, and the [Test Suite](test_suite.qmd) and [PyPI](pypi.qmd) chapters cover testing and building.

## Recap

In this chapter we turned the loose files from the [Shiny for Python](shiny.qmd) chapter into an installable package, one branch at a time:

1. **03.1_pyproject**: a hand written `pyproject.toml` with a `[project]` table replaced `requirements.txt`, and `uv pip install -r pyproject.toml` installed the dependencies.

2. **03.2_uv**: `uv python pin` and `uv sync` handed the environment to `uv`, which created `.python-version`, `.venv/`, and `uv.lock`. Without a `[build-system]` table, `uv` treated `pyap` as a non-package project and installed only its dependencies.

3. **03.3_create-package**: a `[build-system]` table with `uv_build`, an import package in `src/pyap/`, and package imports (`from pyap.utils import scatter_plot`) made `pyap` installable, and `uv sync` installed it in editable mode.

Along the way, we separated modules, import packages, and distributions (which R folds into a single word), and saw why `pyproject.toml` replaced `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, and `requirements.txt`. The project still reads `movies.csv` from the working directory, which we'll fix in the [Data](data.qmd) chapter. In the [Development Workflow](development.qmd) chapter we'll put the package to work with the edit, sync, and run loop.

For more depth on the topics in this chapter, see:

* [Python Packages](https://py-pkgs.org/): the Python counterpart to R Packages, 2ed.
* [Python Packaging User Guide](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/tutorials/packaging-projects/): the official tutorial for building and publishing a package.
* [uv projects documentation](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/): how uv handles `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, and build systems.
